top_choice_rationale: The optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye is a mature, reproduced achievement: the magic-wavelength condition is a predicted cancellation of the trap light shift that experiment confirmed, and Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks in several laboratories now agree at the 1e-18 level, so no single group's modelling carries the result. It has already delivered a millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tighter limits on constants and dark-matter couplings, and a many-body understanding of interaction shifts. Two names give a clean allocation tied to the invention (Katori for the concept, Ye for scaling it to 1e-18 with controlled shifts), provided the expert record on first realisation is checked. The main risks are framing as an instrument and overlap with 2005 and 2012, which a citation centred on the lattice clock answers. I rank the quantum spin Hall proposal second as a serious, defensible prize whose conceptual claim is strong, though its credit chain is incomplete. No award is the weakest option, since two mature candidates are available.
recusal_note: No conflict with Katori or Ye; my collaborators (L'Huillier, the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, Dahlström, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) do not overlap. My field, atomic physics, is close to the lattice clock and I have computed level shifts relevant to such experiments, which may bias me; no recusal apparent from profile.
